body:
_In this Q&A with Michael Hacker, he shares his thoughts on why access to credit secondaries alone is no longer enough, and where he believes real differentiation lies today._

When people talk about private credit, they tend to talk about it as though it’s one big market. They paint the whole market, or certain vintages or strategies, with the same brush. But there are thousands of individual companies underneath, and they’re not all moving in the same direction. Some are doing quite well and derisking their balance sheets, while others are dealing with higher interest costs, weaker earnings, or business models that are changing. The interesting thing is that those differences aren’t always reflected in valuations. That’s really what creates the opportunity for us.

There’s also a bigger picture here. As private credit continues to grow, so does the amount of seasoned credit that managers, banks, and other institutions may want to sell, restructure, or finance. So there’s a structural growth story for credit secondaries alongside the more immediate opportunities we’re seeing today.

Fragmenting means stress is not evenly applied across the market. The pressure is largely concentrated in particular borrowers and sectors. Some people call that dispersion, meaning the gap between stronger and weaker borrowers is widening. From the outside that gap can be hard to see, because lenders are often managing weaker credits through amendments, deferrals, and maturity extensions rather than letting the pressure show up as a default. A single market-wide statistic can make everything look like it’s moving in the same direction when it isn’t.

That’s where buying a portfolio of seasoned loans can have a real advantage over investing in a fund deploying into new-issue loans. Credit secondaries buyers that have years of actual performance to review can see how a company has performed against the original underwriting rather than just relying on projections. And in many transactions, credit secondaries buyers can positively select the loans they want to buy rather than having to take the entire portfolio. Often these are well-priced credits that have performed steadily since being issued.

Headline discounts tend to grab attention, especially from investors, but they can be misleading, or at the very least they don’t tell the whole story. A wide discount can reflect a seller’s own liquidity need rather than anything wrong with the underlying credits, or it can be the market correctly pricing in risk that hasn’t yet shown up in reported performance. The discount alone doesn’t tell you which one you’re looking at.

It’s not necessarily just trying to find the biggest discount, it’s about buying better-than-average credits at market-average prices. If a credit secondaries buyer can select the stronger loans from a portfolio and acquire them at prices that reflect the broader market, that’s potentially a much better investment than buying weaker credits simply because we’re chasing discounts and they look cheap – a classic “value trap”.

Investors can get so focused on the discount that they overlook the underlying yield of the assets. A portfolio of loans paying SOFR + 6.00% is worth considerably more than one paying SOFR + 4.75%, all else equal. The lower-yielding portfolio would need to trade at a meaningfully lower price to generate the same return.

It’s also why we look at the “effective discount” rather than the headline discount, taking into account valuation methodology, manager economics, payment deferrals, and other negotiated terms. For example, an illustrative portfolio priced at 95% of FMV with a high cash yield and a particularly favorable transaction structure may be a materially better investment than one priced at 88% with a greater reliance on payment-in-kind (PIK) interest, which extends the duration of cash flows and increases repayment risk, especially if the latter portfolio’s valuation methodology is more aggressive. Negotiating favorable payment terms or fund structuring is another way to improve returns without necessarily taking more credit risk.

We’re not necessarily trying to call the cycle. What we focus on is how we position ourselves given the risks we perceive in the market. For the past 18 to 24 months, we’ve been moving up the capital structure toward first-lien, senior secured positions, shortening duration, and being more selective about performance and about which opportunities we pursue. Junior risk can still be attractive at the right price, with an appropriate level of cushion, the right structure and alignment, but the bar is higher.

This is also where secondaries compare well with primary direct lending. We may be able to buy a loan originated several years ago, with the benefit of seeing how the company has actually performed, at a discount and with a shorter remaining duration than a newly originated loan. That can create a pretty attractive combination of risk, return and capital velocity.

On transaction type, we’re open to a range of deal settings, whether that’s LP interests, continuation vehicles, or GP strategic solutions. The latter can give us more control over asset selection and structure, but deal type is really just a way of accessing a given risk/return profile, not an end in itself.

Access to transactions still matters, and there’s plenty of competition for assets managed by well-regarded managers, especially in auction settings. While we make sure to look at all situations, the more interesting opportunities for us have often been situations where we’re working directly with a manager or another institution to create a transaction. That might require a bit more effort or creativity from us, but we can influence what we’re buying, how we’re buying it and the economics of the investment. That’s a different proposition from simply showing up at an auction and trying to be the highest bidder.

The other big differentiator is knowing what to buy and what to avoid. Two portfolios can be labeled as direct lending, and they may have similar headline metrics, with managers pointing to the same historical default rates, but the outcomes can be very different. You need to understand how the portfolio is constructed – the individual credits, the quality of the manager, sector concentrations, etc.

That’s where I think experience and information edge can really matter. Ultimately, it’s about having the conviction to pursue the right opportunities, the discipline to pass on others and the ability to structure transactions around the risks.

I think credit secondaries may develop quite differently from private equity secondaries. The opportunity isn’t just LPs selling fund interests or taking liquidity in continuation fund transactions. There is a much broader range of structures holding private credit assets, including enormous portfolios held by banks, insurers, BDCs, and asset managers, and those institutions have lots of reasons to seek liquidity or restructure their exposures.

We believe the continued growth of private credit will create even more opportunities for tailored solutions. I think over time we’ll see credit secondaries become less narrowly defined as a market for trading fund interests and more broadly as a market for providing liquidity and portfolio solutions to institutions holding credit assets. Ultimately, returns ought to increasingly come from selectivity, structuring, and information, rather than simply holding exposure to the asset class.
